slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Stool (clean, dry container; no urine, water or toilet paper)  ·  Units: g/24 h

What it is used for: Stool tests look for blood, bacteria, parasites or signs of disease — for example, when looking for the cause of diarrhea. Finding white blood cells on microscopy helps tell whether diarrhea is due to inflammation in the gut.

Physiology: The normal brown colour of stool comes from bile salts released by the liver. Absorbing fat needs bile, pancreatic enzymes and a normal small intestine; when absorption fails, stool fat rises (steatorrhea).

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 1/5
bullets: Pale or clay-coloured stool may point to a problem in the biliary system: a liver infection that reduces bile production, or blocked bile flow out of the liver. Jaundice and dark urine often occur with it.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 2/5
bullets: Black, tarry stool (melena) most often means bleeding in the upper GI tract — oesophagus, stomach or first part of the small intestine; the blood darkens as it is digested. Red, fresh blood in stool most often comes from the lower GI tract (colon, rectum or anus).

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 3/5
bullets: White blood cells in stool mean there is inflammation in the digestive tract. This helps rule out viral infections, certain bacteria and most parasites. Causes of inflammatory diarrhea include some bacterial infections (C. difficile, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter), inflammatory bowel disease and Entamoeba histolytica; further tests show the exact cause.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 4/5
bullets: Stool fat is checked under a microscope on a single sample, or measured in all stool collected over 24 hours (sometimes 3 days). MedlinePlus gives less than 7 g of fat per 24 hours as normal for the quantitative test. Reduced fat absorption occurs with celiac disease, chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, Crohn disease, biliary strictures or gallstones, and other conditions.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 5/5
bullets: A Gram-stained stool smear is read for the colour, size and shape of bacteria. A normal result shows only the usual ("friendly") gut bacteria. An abnormal result means an intestinal infection may be present; stool culture and other tests help find the cause.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/4
bullets: Pre-analytics: Stool is caught in a clean, dry container or on special paper or plastic wrap over the toilet; never take the sample from toilet water, and keep urine, water and toilet paper out. Label the container with name, date and time, close it tightly and wash hands with soap. If it cannot be returned right away, refrigerate it. For children in diapers, plastic wrap is placed inside the diaper.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/4
bullets: Before a quantitative fat test, eat a normal diet with about 100 g of fat a day for 3 days, then collect all stool over 24 hours (sometimes 3 days) in the containers provided.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/4
bullets: Interferences: Black stool can also come from black licorice, blueberries, blood sausage, iron pills, activated charcoal or bismuth medicines rather than blood; beets and red-coloured foods can make stool look reddish. In these cases the stool is tested chemically for blood.
Enemas, laxatives, mineral oil and too little dietary fat before and during collection interfere with the fat test.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/4
bullets: Limitations: A negative result cannot rule out inflammation: white cells do not last long in stool and may break apart before testing. The test cannot name the exact cause of diarrhea; when the picture is unclear, a stool calprotectin test may be ordered.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 1/4
bullets: Specimen: Stool (2–3 samples a few days apart; in preservative vials when needed)

What it is used for: The test shows whether intestinal parasites are causing symptoms of a gut infection and whether treatment is working. Such symptoms include diarrhea lasting a few days, belly pain, blood or mucus in stool, foul greasy floating stools, nausea, gas, fever and weight loss. It is more likely to be ordered with serious symptoms (dehydration), a weakened immune system, or possible exposure (untreated water, travel, contact with an infected person).

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 2/4
bullets: Physiology: Intestinal parasites live and reproduce in the digestive system; they and their eggs are passed in stool. Invisible traces of contaminated stool reach water, soil, food and surfaces, and infection follows when they are swallowed. Some worms, such as hookworms, enter through the skin, especially when walking barefoot.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 3/4
bullets: A wet mount shows protozoan trophozoites, cysts and oocysts as well as helminth eggs and larvae: a small amount of stool is placed on a slide and, if fairly solid, mixed with a drop or two of saline; ideally two smears are made on one slide, one stained with iodine. The whole coverslip is scanned systematically with the 10× objective. Permanent stained slides identify trophozoites and cysts to species — at least 200–300 oil-immersion fields are examined. Size is a key feature, so the microscope is calibrated with an ocular micrometer.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 4/4
bullets: Direct (wet) microscopy is done in two drops: saline (warmed to 37 °C) shows motile trophozoites, Lugol’s iodine (iodine–acetic acid) shows cyst nuclei clearly — iodine immobilises trophozoites. Use liquid or mucoid stool for trophozoites and formed stool for eggs.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result
cols: A positive result means parasites and/or eggs were found — there are intestinal parasites. The report also gives the type and how many were seen. Treatment depends on the parasite and general health; plenty of fluids help prevent dehydration from diarrhea and vomiting.

A negative result means no parasites or eggs were found: either there are none, or too few were in the sample. Parasites are not shed in stool every day, so collection is repeated after a negative first exam — CDC advises examining three specimens passed 2–3 days apart when possible.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/9
bullets: Pre-analytics: Collect stool in a dry, clean, leak-proof container with no urine, water or soil. Fresh stool is examined, processed or preserved immediately; an unpreserved specimen kept only under refrigeration is suitable for antigen testing only. Without a kit, the specimen is split between 10% formalin and PVA (polyvinyl alcohol): one volume of stool to three volumes of preservative, mixed well, with formed stool broken up.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/9
bullets: Collect stool in a clean, dry, lidded container without preservative; no urine (not from a bedpan), and include any worms or segments passed. WHO advises examining it within 1–4 hours and, if several arrive together, looking first at liquid and blood- or mucus-stained stools — motile amoebae die quickly. Lyubina (1984) and Aripova (2007) also reject matchboxes or paper.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/9
bullets: For shipping to a distant laboratory a preservative is added: 10% formalin (for wet mounts and sedimentation), PVA (for permanent stains such as trichrome), MIF or SAF/TIF mixtures. Dadayev (2004) also notes that stool for amoebiasis must be preserved (or delivered quickly).

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/9
bullets: Interferences: Certain drugs and compounds make stool unsatisfactory for examination: antacids, kaolin, mineral oil and other oily materials, non-absorbable antidiarrheals, barium or bismuth (7–10 days to clear), antimicrobial agents (2–3 weeks) and gallbladder dyes (3 weeks). Collect before they are given or wait until their effects have passed.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/9
bullets: Limitations: Each preservative has drawbacks: formalin preserves helminth eggs, larvae and cysts well but not trophozoite morphology, and long fixation can interfere with PCR; PVA preserves trophozoites and cysts well but not helminth eggs or larvae, and is unsuitable for concentration procedures. Using both is therefore recommended. If PCR is needed, the specimen is collected to its specific requirements.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 6/9
bullets: For pinworm, a stool test is usually not useful — stool rarely contains enough eggs; the perianal tape test is used instead.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 7/9
bullets: Concentration is needed when parasites are few. In flotation (e.g., Willis saturated NaCl; zinc sulfate) eggs rise in a dense solution: good for hookworm, Ascaris, Hymenolepis, Taenia and Trichuris eggs, but not for fluke and schistosome eggs, Strongyloides larvae or protozoa — some eggs do not float and cyst and egg walls may collapse. Sedimentation (formalin–ether or formalin–ethyl acetate) recovers more species, is easier, and CDC recommends it for general laboratories; ethyl acetate is less flammable than ether.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 8/9
bullets: In the Kato (Kato–Katz) thick smear about 0.5 g of sieved stool is cleared under glycerol-soaked cellophane (with malachite green or methylene blue); it detects and counts helminth eggs, especially Schistosoma, and slides can be stored and shipped. It is unsuitable for strongyloidiasis, enterobiasis and protozoa.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 9/9
bullets: No single method finds every parasite: always do direct microscopy before concentration (motile forms are not seen in concentrated preparations). If the result is negative, the doctor may request repeat samples on other days.

slides.title: Fecal occult blood test (FOBT/FIT)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Stool (on a card or in a tube from the kit, from 1–3 bowel movements)

What it is used for: The test is mostly used to screen people without symptoms for colorectal cancer; at average risk, screening usually starts at age 45. It is also used when GI bleeding is suspected, to look for the cause of anemia, and to help tell irritable bowel syndrome (usually no bleeding) from inflammatory bowel disease (bleeding likely).

slides.title: Fecal occult blood test (FOBT/FIT)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: "Occult" blood is blood you cannot see. Blood in stool means bleeding somewhere in the digestive tract. Causes include polyps, hemorrhoids, diverticulosis, ulcers, ulcerative colitis and colorectal cancer.

There are two main types. The guaiac test (gFOBT) detects blood chemically with guaiac and usually needs samples from two or three separate bowel movements. The fecal immunochemical test (FIT, iFOBT) uses an antibody that binds hemoglobin in stool, is better at finding blood, and needs one to three samples depending on the brand.

slides.title: Fecal occult blood test (FOBT/FIT)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result
bullets: Positive result: A positive result means there is likely bleeding somewhere in the digestive tract, but not necessarily cancer: ulcers, hemorrhoids, polyps and benign tumors can also cause it. More tests are needed to find where and why; the most common follow-up is colonoscopy.

slides.title: Fecal occult blood test (FOBT/FIT)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/5
bullets: Pre-analytics: Each kit has its own instructions, and following them exactly matters. Usually stool is caught on special paper, plastic wrap or in a clean dry container (for gFOBT, keep urine out), a sample is taken with the kit's stick or brush from the indicated place, smeared on a card or put in a tube, labeled and sealed, repeated with the next bowel movement if required, and returned as directed.

slides.title: Fecal occult blood test (FOBT/FIT)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/5
bullets: Diet depends on the test type: the immunochemical test (FIT) uses antibodies specific to haemoglobin protein and typically needs no diet or medicine changes. The guaiac test (gFOBT) also detects haem from food, so red meat, some vegetables and medicines may be restricted beforehand. The 3–5-day diet in the textbook applies only to chemical (guaiac or benzidine-type) tests.

slides.title: Fecal occult blood test (FOBT/FIT)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/5
bullets: Interferences: Many tests need no special preparation. For some guaiac tests, though, foods and medicines affect the result, and the provider will say what to avoid and for how long — for example NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin; do not stop aspirin taken for the heart without asking), vitamin C over 250 mg a day (supplements, juices, fruit), red meat (beef, lamb, liver) and certain raw fruits and vegetables.

slides.title: Fecal occult blood test (FOBT/FIT)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/5
bullets: Limitations: The test alone cannot diagnose any condition: if blood is found, other tests are needed to find the cause. When used for screening, it must be repeated every year. Other screening options include the stool DNA test (FIT-DNA), colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy and CT colonography.

slides.title: Fecal occult blood test (FOBT/FIT)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/5
bullets: The benzidine (Gregersen) test of old textbooks is no longer used: WHO does not recommend benzidine because it has been shown to be carcinogenic. Remaining chemical tests are the aminopyrine and guaiac tests, which need a diet (WHO, aminopyrine test: 1 day without meat or iron tablets; older textbooks: 2–3 days); the immunochemical test (FIT) is specific for human haemoglobin and needs no diet.

slides.title: Saline wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Motile trophozoites, moderate numbers of eggs and cysts, red cells, fat
Limitations: May miss scanty parasites; use liquid stool and saline warmed to 37 °C for trophozoites

slides.title: Iodine (Lugol) mount
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Cyst nuclei and glycogen vacuoles; telling Giardia and amoeba cysts apart
Limitations: Trophozoites stop moving — check motility in saline

slides.title: Kato (Kato–Katz) thick smear
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Helminth eggs, especially Schistosoma; egg counts; slides can be stored and shipped
Limitations: Not for strongyloidiasis, enterobiasis or protozoa

slides.title: Flotation
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Light eggs rise in a dense solution (saturated NaCl — Willis; zinc sulfate): hookworm, Ascaris, Hymenolepis, Taenia, Trichuris
Limitations: Fluke and schistosome eggs, Strongyloides larvae, protozoa; cyst and egg walls may collapse

slides.title: Sedimentation
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Formalin–ether or formalin–ethyl acetate: most eggs, larvae and cysts; CDC recommends it for general laboratories
Limitations: Motile forms are not seen — do a wet mount first; ether is flammable, ethyl acetate is safer

slides.title: Preservatives (shipping)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool · 1/2
bullets: 10% formalin — for wet mounts and sedimentation; preserves eggs and cysts well, trophozoites less so.
PVA — for permanent (trichrome) stains; MIF, SAF or TIF — mixtures for wet mounts.

slides.title: Preservatives (shipping)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool · 2/2
bullets: Fresh stool without preservative is examined within 1–4 hours; liquid and blood- or mucus-stained stool first.

slides.title: Pinworm: adhesive tape
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: Pinworm eggs are scarce in stool — collect them with tape from the perianal skin.
In the morning before washing or using the toilet; repeat on three consecutive days.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A · Oral question
rows: fecal fat >7 g/24 h; elastase <100 µg/g (100–200 indeterminate) g/24 h; µg/g
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

slides.title: A patient had a barium x-ray yesterday and today's stool is sent for parasites. What is right?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Wait until the barium effect clears (7–10 days), then collect
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. Collect before barium or after its effects have passed.

Basis: CDC DPDx: barium or bismuth makes stool unsatisfactory; 7–10 days are needed for the effect to clear.

slides.title: Which advice before a guaiac test (gFOBT) matches MedlinePlus?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Avoid red meat and vitamin C over 250 mg a day for the period your provider specifies
Stop heart aspirin on your own
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. These affect guaiac test results.

Basis: NSAIDs, vitamin C over 250 mg/day, red meat and certain raw fruits and vegetables affect guaiac tests.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of stool examination?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Stool analysis helps to assess digestive function (stomach, pancreas, liver-biliary tract, intestine), inflammation, bleeding and infections/infestations.

2. Coprology: macroscopic (amount, consistency, color, mucus, blood, worms), chemical (pH, occult blood, stercobilin, bilirubin), microscopic (muscle fibers, neutral fat and fatty acids, starch, fiber, leukocytes, erythrocytes, parasites).

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of stool examination?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 3. Modern targeted tests: occult blood – immunochemical test (FIT, colorectal cancer screening), calprotectin (intestinal inflammation), elastase-1 (pancreatic exocrine insufficiency), H. pylori antigen, pathogen antigens and PCR panels.
4. Steatorrhea: screening with Sudan III, quantitative fecal fat (>7 g/day) – reference.
5. Interpretation with clinical data and diet; correct specimen collection and rapid delivery.

slides.title: Macroscopic and chemical examination of stool. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Macroscopic: amount, shape and consistency, color (acholic – bile duct obstruction; black/tarry – upper GI bleeding or iron/bismuth; bright red blood – lower parts), odor, mucus, pus, undigested food, worms and segments.

2. Chemical: pH, occult blood – instead of guaiac tests (pseudoperoxidase; diet and drugs interfere), an immunochemical test specific for human hemoglobin (FIT) – no dietary restriction, more sensitive; stercobilin (absence – obstruction), bilirubin (when intestinal flora is disturbed).
3. Special protein markers: calprotectin – intestinal inflammation (distinguishing IBD from IBS), elastase-1 – pancreatic exocrine function.

slides.title: Macroscopic and chemical examination of stool. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Fat digestion: screening with Sudan stain, quantitative fecal fat.
5. Clinical significance: source of bleeding, malabsorption and maldigestion, inflammation, tumor screening (FIT).

slides.title: Microscopic examination of stool. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Preparations: native (physiological saline), Lugol (starch, iodophilic flora, protozoan cysts), Sudan III (neutral fat), with acetic acid (fatty acids, soaps).

2. Food remnants: muscle fibers (creatorrhea – gastric and pancreatic insufficiency), neutral fat (steatorrhea – lipase insufficiency), fatty acids and soaps (bile insufficiency, impaired intestinal absorption), starch (amylorrhea), digestible fiber.

slides.title: Microscopic examination of stool. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 3. Elements of the intestinal wall: mucus, leukocytes (inflammation – colitis, invasive diarrhea), erythrocytes, epithelium; Charcot-Leyden crystals (eosinophilic inflammation, parasites).
4. Parasites: eggs and larvae of helminths, vegetative forms and cysts of protozoa (fresh specimen, enrichment methods if needed).
5. A tentative conclusion based on coprological syndromes; for confirmation – special tests (elastase, calprotectin, antigen/PCR).
